clue.text: Drug supplier cut short proposal in church

indicators.note: Cutting a word short takes its last letter off, so it goes in one letter lighter than it came.
It marks an insertion: the shortened word ends up inside the word named after it.

parts.note: the Church of England shortens to CE, and the two letters part company to let something sit between them
a proposal is an offer, docked of its final letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dealer collared in a pew, which is why the real definition arrives so quietly: the drug in question is caffeine.
explanation.definitionFit: Caffeine is a drug and this is the cup that delivers it, so the definition names the thing by what it hands you.

clue.text: Member of nobility beheaded 9 in castle

indicators.note: A beheading takes the top letter off a word, which in a down entry is the letter that would have gone in first.

parts.note: CH is the Companion of Honour, the crossword's two-letter grandee — an order in the sovereign's gift, which is the loose sense of rank the clue leans on
9 across is cake, and the French one — a gateau, to suit the French surface — gives up its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference usually hands over a word; this one hands over a category, and the letters only come out if you pick the French member of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word taken straight into English means a castle, or the grand turreted country house that grew out of one.

clue.text: Imagined being a queen in fancy clothing

indicators.note: It marks the insertion: what is named before it is pushed inside what is named after it.
Clothes go round the outside, so this word takes only the outer letters of the word in front of it and wraps them round the rest.

parts.note: only the outside of the word is kept — the F at the front, the Y at the back, and the middle three dropped
the article is taken at face value
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the crossword's standing queen

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that nobody is wearing anything: 'clothing' is an instruction about the outside of a word, and the fancy dress is the surface's own.
explanation.definitionFit: An imagined being is a creature that exists only in the mind — the fairy of folklore, spelled here the old Spenserian way.

clue.text: Oriental festival ending in confusion

parts.note: the church's chief festival, the one the calendar is built around

indicators.note: On the surface the party dissolves into chaos; as an instruction it asks only for the letter the next word finishes with.

parts.note: the final letter of the word is all that is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: A festival collapsing into confusion is a fine picture, and the picture is all the surface is for — the setter's festival is a perfectly orderly one.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Oriental' is the older adjective for the east, from the Latin for the rising sun, so it swaps in wherever this one does.

clue.text: Comic character in yellow?

parts.note: 'character' asks for a single letter of type, and which one is left to the crossing letters
cream is a pale yellow, and the question mark is the setter owning up to a shade standing in for the colour

explanation.walkthrough: Definition and wordplay both live in informal English: a hilarious person is 'a comic', and the same person is 'a scream'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Comic' used as a noun is a funny person, and this is the colloquial word for exactly that — someone or something hilarious.

clue.text: Incentive rising in motor racing

indicators.note: A down entry that rises reads bottom to top, so the letters found here go into the grid the other way round.
It says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow, waiting to be lifted out rather than built.

parts.note: six consecutive letters straddle the gap between these two words, and the entry climbs through them

explanation.walkthrough: Motor racing is a whole world of sponsorship and inducements, which is why the phrase reads as scenery instead of as the place the letters are lying.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive is the carrot of 'carrot and stick' — the reward dangled in front of someone to get them moving.

clue.text: Old joke by judge giving pardon

parts.note: ex- is the prefix meaning former, the crossword's standing 'old'
a joke is 'a good one' — have you heard the one about...
to rate something is to judge it, to set a value on it

explanation.walkthrough: Three everyday words in a row and not one instruction: the only real difficulty is seeing that the middle piece is a noun meaning a gag.
explanation.definitionFit: To pardon is to clear someone of blame officially, which is what this verb does — declaring a person not at fault after all.

clue.text: Mother has fixed idea about River Island

indicators.note: Something fixed has been taken apart and put back together differently, and that is what happens to the letters beside it.

parts.note: MA is the nursery word for mother

indicators.note: A piece put about another closes round it, so the re-set letters wrap the single one.

parts.note: the four letters of the notion are re-set around R, the map-maker's river

explanation.walkthrough: The surface's River Island is a high-street shop, so the capital letters mislead twice: the clue wants only R for river, and 'Island' is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Island' is the plain sense — the Atlantic island Portugal settled, which then lent its name to both a wine and a cake.

clue.text: ELO apparently created a bit of atmosphere

indicators.note: What is created is built afresh out of the material to hand, so these letters are made into something new.

parts.note: the band's three initials and the adverb behind them supply all thirteen letters

explanation.walkthrough: Edward Appleton took a Nobel for finding this region of the ionosphere, the one that bounces short-wave radio back down. 'Apparently' looks like a hedge and is really fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: 'A bit of atmosphere' is literal, not figurative: the answer names one measurable layer of the upper air, high above the weather.

clue.text: Greek actress partly redirected Hollywood production?

indicators.note: Only part of the words beside it is wanted, the standing signal that the letters are already there to be picked out.
Redirected traffic goes the other way, so the run of letters is read back to front.

parts.note: four letters in a row straddle the gap between the two words, and they are read from right to left

explanation.walkthrough: This is the clue the rest of the grid leans on, so it pays to spot the trick early: the question mark is doing a lot of work for one small joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Hollywood judges the baking on Bake Off, so what this Hollywood 'produces' is baked rather than filmed — hence the question mark.

clue.text: Poor US Feds demolished Fruit & Nuts?

indicators.note: Demolish something and every piece is still there, just no longer in the order it was built in.

parts.note: the ten letters of the three words are the whole of the material

explanation.walkthrough: 'Demolished' works both ways round: the agents are wrecked on the surface and the plate of food is demolished at the table, while the letters quietly change places.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark admits examples rather than a synonym: berries and almonds are among the foods sold as unusually nutrient-dense.

clue.text: Peter Kay at last playing key characters again

indicators.note: Letters at play are letters not staying put, so the name in front of it is free to be reordered.
It points at the very end of the word before it, so only that final letter joins in.

parts.note: the five letters of the first name are the bulk of the fodder
the last letter of the surname makes up the six

explanation.walkthrough: Peter Kay is a comedian and 'playing' is what comedians do, so the whole first half reads as showbusiness rather than as raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Key' is a verb here — to key characters is to type them — so keying them again is precisely the instruction the answer carries.

clue.text: Briefly visited butcher's next to Scottish city

indicators.note: It puts the two pieces side by side in the order given, with neither going inside the other.

parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang, and the rhyming half is never spoken: a butcher's hook
Edinburgh in its dictionary short form

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are abbreviations of a kind — one by slang, one by the dictionary — and neither is signalled, which is what makes an eight-letter answer feel like a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: To look in on someone is to call round briefly, so the definition matches a whole-phrase idiom rather than a single word.

clue.text: American making a comeback with bronze in former territory

indicators.note: Something that comes back retraces its steps, so these two letters are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: the US, turned round

indicators.note: It marks the insertion: the piece named before it goes inside the word named after it.

parts.note: 'late' is the word for former — the late chairman — and it opens after one letter
a tan is the bronze a fortnight in the sun leaves you with

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate liberties with plain words — a country as two letters, a colour as a verb's worth of skin, and 'former' as an adjective for the dead — all inside one smooth sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A territory named by whoever rules it: this is the state a sultan governs, as a kingdom is a king's.

clue.text: Wooden bench with section removed for brewing accessory

indicators.note: What is removed leaves the letters altogether, so the piece named just before it is taken out of what came earlier.

parts.note: 'wooden' points at a particular timber rather than at a quality
a settle is a long high-backed bench, here short of the letter named next
section abbreviates to S, and that is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the real disguise: (3,6) cuts through the middle of the timber, so neither half of the answer lines up with either half of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewing accessory is anything the tea-making needs, and this is the vessel that boils the water for it.

clue.text: 9 sailors from the East

indicators.note: In an across row the east is the right-hand end, so reading from there means reading the letters backwards.

parts.note: an AB is an able seaman, and the plural asks for a pair of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'From the East' looks like scenery about foreign ports and is really a compass direction telling you which way along the row to read.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 across is cake, and this is one: the small yeast cake, usually soaked in rum, that Poland and France both claim.

clue.text: 9 having afternoon in bed

indicators.note: It marks an insertion: the single letter before it is dropped inside the word after it.

parts.note: a cot is a bed, and it opens after two letters to take the insertion
'afternoon' does loose work here, standing for a bare A — timetable shorthand rather than a dictionary abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is a verb here, not a noun: cake is what dried mud does to a boot, and that is the sense the definition wants.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 across is cake, and to cake something is to coat it — mud cakes a boot exactly as paint coats a wall.

clue.text: More than one whoopsie from Business Secretary's empty threats about women

indicators.note: A word emptied out keeps only its shell, the first and last letters, and loses everything between them.

parts.note: a business is a company, CO
W is the standing abbreviation for women
a secretary is a PA, a personal assistant

indicators.note: Letters placed about something go round it, so the pieces already found open up to admit what follows.

parts.note: the shell of the word, once the middle has been emptied out

explanation.walkthrough: Every piece here is a political abbreviation except the last, which is the same word made hollow — and the childish definition is the only plain English in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Whoopsie' is nursery language for droppings, and these are the cow's: the flat pancakes left across a field.

clue.text: Great-niece unfortunately lacking the focus of Blake Lively

indicators.note: Things that go unfortunately do not come out in the order they were meant to, which is the licence to reorder the letters.
The focus of a word is its centre, so the middle letter of the name is the one meant.
What is lacking is missing from the letters, so the piece named after it never joins the mix.

parts.note: the fodder, once the letter named next has gone
the centre of the five-letter name is A, and that is the letter left out

explanation.walkthrough: Blake Lively is one name doing two jobs: the surname defines the answer while the first name gives up its middle letter to the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Lively' is the surface's actress, but as a plain adjective it means full of energy, which is what the answer means too.

clue.text: Heart of Hugh Bonneville ultimately captured by fancy-free Paddington Bear?

indicators.note: At the very end — so only the final letter of the name in front of it is wanted.
Whatever captures something closes round it, so the letters found so far go inside the piece named next.
To fancy something up is to dress it differently, and letters dressed differently come out in a new order.

parts.note: the four letters are re-set, and then they open up to take the rest

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, so the letters at the centre are the ones taken.

parts.note: the middle pair of a four-letter name
the very last letter of the surname

explanation.walkthrough: Two actors' names and neither matters: only Hugh's middle and Bonneville's tail are used, and the bear from Darkest Peru does the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Paddington arrives from Peru with a label asking someone to please look after him, which is a refugee's story.

clue.text: Imagines day in Rome includes scoff

indicators.note: What includes something holds it inside, so the word before it opens to take the word after.

parts.note: the Ides is a Roman day of the month — beware the Ides of March — and it splits after two letters
to scoff is to eat, and greedily

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves need re-reading: 'day in Rome' is not a date but the Latin name for one, and 'scoff' is a meal rather than a sneer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ideate is to form ideas — the psychologist's and the management consultant's verb for thinking something up.

clue.text: Wipe bum

definitions.meaning: the first verb: to wipe a surface down with something soft and absorbent
the second verb: to cadge, as in bumming a cigarette off a stranger

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two verbs, no wordplay at all — and the shortest clue in the grid is also the one most likely to be read as a rude joke.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is to wipe something down; the other is to cadge, which is what bumming a fiver off a friend amounts to.

clue.text: Rock maybe cut mountain climber

indicators.note: It flags an example rather than a synonym: what follows is one kind of the thing named, not the thing itself.
A cut word loses its end, so the mountain here arrives one letter shorter.

parts.note: seaside rock is a stick of boiled sugar — one kind of confection, not a stone
a mountain is a peak, docked of its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: Two plain words both need re-reading: the rock is edible and the climber is rooted. Nothing in the surface is what it first appears to be.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Climber' is the gardener's sense — a plant that runs up canes or trellis — and this fragrant annual is one of the commonest.

clue.text: Rod Hull's beginning to get into battered fries

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its first letter, and that is all this takes from the surname.
It puts the letter just found in among the others, so the single letter joins the material being reordered.
Something battered has lost its shape, which is exactly what happens to the order of these letters.

parts.note: the first letter of the surname
the five letters of the chips, which reorder around the letter joining them

explanation.walkthrough: Rod Hull and his emu carry the surface, and only the H of Hull is needed. 'Battered fries' is a chip-shop picture doing an anagram's job.
explanation.definitionFit: In angling a 'rod' is the person holding one — a fishery sells so many rods a day — so the word names the angler by the tackle.

clue.text: Finally calls 999?

indicators.note: It asks for the very end of the word beside it, so only that last letter is written down.

parts.note: the last letter of the word, and nothing else from it
a 99 is the ice cream served in a wafer with a flake pushed into it

explanation.walkthrough: Three nines do two jobs: the first two are the ice-cream 99, and the last one is the cross-reference at 9 across. The question mark covers the cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 across is cake, and this counts as one: a small plain cake, baked flat and split for jam and cream.

clue.text: Austrian barman hiding half of national treasure in 9

indicators.note: What is hidden goes inside something else, so the name before it wraps around the letters that follow.
Exactly half the letters are taken, counted rather than trimmed: six of the twelve, from the front.

parts.note: the Austrian is Alban Berg, the Viennese composer, and his name splits after one letter; 'barman' is the surface's own man behind the bar
the nation's treasure is David Attenborough, and his twelve letters are cut down the middle

explanation.walkthrough: Two famous names, one inside the other, which is how the surface gets to be about smuggling. Both are so well known that neither needs a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 across is cake, and this is one by name: the pink-and-yellow chequered sponge wrapped in marzipan.

clue.text: Attila the Hun originally behind old curse

indicators.note: At their origins — so each of the three words in the name gives up only its opening letter.
What stands behind something follows it, so the initials line up after the single letter.

parts.note: O is the crossword's standing letter for old
the opening letters of all three words, the little one included

explanation.walkthrough: Attila is a good villain for a bad word, and the trap is 'the': every word of the name is needed, including the one you would skip.
explanation.definitionFit: A curse is a swear word, and that is one of this word's two senses — the profanity, not the promise sworn in court.

clue.text: Tennis player getting journalist stoned

parts.note: a ranked player at a tournament is a seed — the top seed, the third seed
ED is the editor, the crossword's standing journalist

explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are conventions worth owning for good: the ranked player and the editor turn up in a grid most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Stoned' of a fruit means the stones have been taken out, and doing the same to grapes or raisins is called seeding them.

clue.text: Joe Swash oddly hoarding article of Spanish treasure

definitions.note: Treasure is a mass noun, so one word covers any number of pieces — which is how a singular-looking definition fairly defines a plural answer.

indicators.note: Odd here counts positions rather than describing behaviour: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters.
A hoard is kept inside, so the letters just found close round whatever comes next.

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of the two names read straight through
'el' is the Spanish for 'the', and it slips inside

explanation.walkthrough: Counting through 'Joe Swash' letter by letter is the whole job, and the Spanish article hides in the sentence without disturbing the surface at all.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Treasure' is the collective word for precious stones and worked metal, so it names a hoard made of exactly these.
